question: What is the main goal of a National Health Policy?

options.A: To exclusively control pharmaceutical manufacturing prices
options.B: To outline healthcare priorities and resource allocation strategies
options.C: To license private medical practitioners across the country
options.D: To manage hospital infrastructure funding in rural areas

explanation: A National Health Policy sets the main framework for national healthcare needs, guiding how resources and services are distributed to improve public health. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must the National Drug Policy match closely with the National Health Policy?

options.A: Medications are essential tools needed to achieve broader health goals
options.B: Drug policies operate independently from clinical health interventions
options.C: Hospitals cannot purchase equipment without prior drug policy clearance
options.D: Pharmaceutical companies fund the implementation of national health budgets

explanation: Good healthcare needs medicines, so drug policies must line up with overall health goals to successfully treat illnesses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: When was Nigeria's very first National Drug Policy launched?
explanation: Nigeria introduced its first official National Drug Policy in 1990 to fight fake drugs and chaotic drug importation. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: What major problem led to the creation of early drug policies in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive government funding for international drug importation
options.B: A complete lack of qualified doctors in urban teaching hospitals
options.C: Rampant fake products and an unregulated open drug market
options.D: An absolute surplus of locally manufactured pharmaceutical products

explanation: Unregulated open drug markets and fake medications caused serious health crises, prompting the government to create official drug policies. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a main goal of the National Drug Policy?

options.A: Eliminating all private pharmacies from urban areas
options.B: Promoting the rational use of essential medicines
options.C: Mandating free herbal remedies in tertiary hospitals
options.D: Increasing international importation of luxury cosmetics

explanation: Rational drug use ensures patients get the right medicines for their clinical needs at the correct doses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why is boosting local drug manufacturing a key goal in Nigeria's drug policy?

options.A: To ensure that nurses can manufacture intravenous fluids in wards
options.B: To reduce heavy reliance on foreign drug importation and stabilize supply
options.C: To completely ban foreign pharmaceutical companies from operating locally
options.D: To eliminate the need for quality control regulatory agencies

explanation: Making drugs locally protects the country from global supply shortages and foreign exchange price changes. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which agency handles drug manufacturing and importation rules in Nigeria?
explanation: NAFDAC stands for the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, which monitors drug safety and manufacturing standards. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the specific role of the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria?

options.A: Manufacturing essential vaccines for rural primary healthcare centers
options.B: Regulating the training and professional practice of pharmacists
options.C: Conducting clinical trials on new surgical techniques in teaching hospitals
options.D: Setting international pricing standards for imported medical equipment

explanation: The Pharmacists Council of Nigeria handles professional standards, licensing, and training for pharmacy staff rather than checking manufactured products. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: How are essential medicines defined in national health and drug policies?

options.A: Medicines that satisfy the priority healthcare needs of the population
options.B: Traditional herbal extracts prepared by local community healers
options.C: Experimental medications tested only in tertiary research institutions
options.D: Expensive brand-name drugs imported exclusively from Western countries

explanation: Essential medicines are chosen based on common illnesses, safety, how well they work, and affordability. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: A patient cannot afford prescribed antibiotics out of pocket. Which policy helps fix this issue?

options.A: Direct referral to private international pharmaceutical consultants
options.B: Increasing import tariffs on raw pharmaceutical ingredients
options.C: National Health Insurance Authority coverage schemes
options.D: Immediate suspension of local generic drug manufacturing plants

explanation: Health insurance helps protect patients from heavy out-of-pocket costs by covering or subsidizing essential medicines. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: What technology helps patients check if their drugs are real in Nigeria?

options.A: Microscopic chemical analysis at patient bedsides
options.B: Mandatory DNA sequencing at local retail pharmacies
options.C: Biometric fingerprint scanning for medication purchase

explanation: NAFDAC set up mobile authentication services that let buyers scratch a panel and text a pin to check if a drug is real via SMS. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why are fake or substandard drugs very dangerous for treating infections?

options.A: They foster antimicrobial resistance and cause treatment failure
options.B: They immediately cure infections without requiring medical supervision
options.C: They eliminate the need for diagnostic laboratory testing in clinics
options.D: They reduce the cost of healthcare services for impoverished patients

explanation: Substandard drugs have weak active ingredients, which fail to kill germs and instead help germs build resistance to future treatments. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do nurses help with national pharmacovigilance?

options.A: By manufacturing intravenous replacement fluids in hospital wards
options.B: By setting the retail prices for generic drugs in community pharmacies
options.C: By reporting adverse drug reactions to regulatory authorities
options.D: By importing essential medications directly from foreign manufacturers

explanation: Pharmacovigilance is about tracking and reporting bad drug reactions, and frontline nurses play a big role in spotting and reporting them. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h7)

question: A nurse sees that new oxytocin vials do not have NAFDAC registration numbers. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Administer the medication quickly before supervisors notice the anomaly
options.B: Sell the unregistered vials to patients at a discounted hospital price
options.C: Store the medication in the ward refrigerator for emergency use only
options.D: Quarantine the batch and report it through institutional channels

explanation: Unregistered drugs are unsafe. Nurses must hold off on giving them, isolate the bad stock, and report it right away. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h7)
